speaker: student
text: Exercise 1 asks for the two phases of classification. I keep wanting to say 'training and testing' — is that wrong?

speaker: tutor
text: It is close but not quite the right vocabulary. The two phases are the learning phase, where a model is applied to unlabeled instances to predict their class, and the querying phase (also called the classification or deduction phase), where a learning algorithm builds a model from labeled training data. 'Training and testing' describes how you evaluate the result, not the two conceptual phases themselves.

speaker: student
text: Okay, so is the learning set the same thing as the training set then?

speaker: tutor
text: Not quite — the learning set is the whole pool of labeled data you have available. You then split it into a training set, used to build the model, and a test set, held back to check how well that model generalizes. The split matters because if you evaluated on the same data you trained on, you would be measuring how well the model memorized the data, not how well it performs on new cases.

speaker: student
text: For the borrower table, is Defaulted Borrower the target attribute because it's the last column, or for some other reason?

speaker: tutor
text: Column position is irrelevant — it is the target attribute because it is the variable the model is built to predict, and it must be discrete with a fixed, known set of class values, here Y and N. Home Owner, Marital Status, Level of Education, and Annual Income are input attributes that describe each instance; the target is whatever the induction step is trying to output.

speaker: student
text: For Table 1, I said Home Owner and Marital Status are categorical, Level of Education is categorical too since it's words, and Annual Income is numerical. Is that right?

speaker: tutor
text: That is all correct. Level of Education is written as words like Low, Moderate, and High, so it is plain categorical exactly as you said, the same as Marital Status. The distinction is about whether the values are text or numbers, not about any ordering among them.

speaker: student
text: For the doctor example — 99% reliable test, 1% of people actually sick, patient tests positive — my gut says the probability they're sick should be close to 99%.

speaker: tutor
text: That is the classic base-rate trap, and it is a good one to get wrong once. Bayes' theorem gives P(sick|+) = P(+|sick)P(+) / P(sick), where P(sick) sums the positive-test probability over both sick and healthy people. Plugging in: (0.99 × 0.01) / (0.99 × 0.01 + 0.01 × 0.99) = 0.0099 / 0.0198 = 0.5. So it's actually a coin flip — because sickness is so rare, the much larger pool of healthy people still produces about as many false positives as the small sick pool produces true positives.

speaker: student
text: So how does the Naive Bayes classifier actually decide the class, and why is it called 'naive'?

speaker: tutor
text: In the classification phase it picks the class y that maximizes P(y) · Π P(xi|y) over all attributes xi, using Bayes' theorem and dropping the shared denominator P(X) since it is the same for every class. It is called 'naive' because that product form assumes all attributes are conditionally independent given the class — in reality Home Owner and Marital Status might interact, but the model pretends they don't, which keeps the math tractable at some cost in accuracy.

speaker: student
text: Annual Income isn't categorical, so how does Naive Bayes get a probability for something like Income = 90?

speaker: tutor
text: For a numeric attribute you don't count frequencies — you estimate a class-conditional density instead. The usual choice is a Gaussian: for each class, compute the mean μ and variance σ² of that attribute among instances of that class, then plug your value into the normal density formula f(x|μ,σ²) = (1/√(πσ²)) · exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)). That density value stands in for P(x|class) in the product.

speaker: student
text: Let me try the priors and conditionals for X = (Home Owner = N, Marital Status = Married, Income = 90). P(No) should be 7/10 and P(Yes) 3/10, right?

speaker: tutor
text: Correct — 7 of the 10 borrowers are No, 3 are Yes, so those are your priors. For the conditionals given No: Home Owner = N occurs in 4 of the 7 No-instances, so P(HO=N|No) = 4/7, and Married occurs in 4 of the 7 No-instances too, so P(MS=Married|No) = 4/7. Now check the Yes side the same way before we plug everything in.

speaker: student
text: For DB=Yes, all three instances have Home Owner = N, so P(HO=N|Yes) = 3/3 = 1. But none of them have Marital Status = Married — they're Divorced, Single, Single.

speaker: tutor
text: That's exactly the trap this dataset is built to expose. P(MS=Married|Yes) = 0/3 = 0, and because the naive Bayes formula multiplies all the conditional probabilities together, that single zero collapses the entire P(X|Yes) term to zero — no matter how strongly the income term might have pointed toward Yes. Without any correction, the instance gets classified as No purely because Married never happened to appear in the small Yes group during training, not because the evidence genuinely rules it out.

speaker: student
text: So does the Laplace estimate fix that zero and maybe even flip the classification?

speaker: tutor
text: It does both. Laplace smoothing is applied after the full product has been formed: you first multiply the raw conditional probabilities together, and only then add one pseudo-count to the resulting posterior and adjust its denominator, P(v|class) = (count(v,class) + 1) / (count(class) + k), where k is the number of possible values for that attribute. For Married given Yes, that's (0+1)/(3+3) = 1/6 instead of 0. Once you carry that through the full product for both classes, the Yes posterior actually overtakes No — with the Gaussian income term centered right at 90 for the Yes class, the smoothed evidence tips the classification from No to Yes. That flip is the whole point of doing Q5 after Q4.

speaker: student
text: Exercise 3 wants me to explain a problem with using Information Gain as a splitting criterion. What's the issue?

speaker: tutor
text: Information Gain is biased toward attributes with many distinct values. An attribute like a customer ID column, where every instance has a unique value, produces a split with one instance per branch — each child node is perfectly pure, so the gain looks huge, even though the split is useless for predicting new instances. The measure rewards fragmentation, not genuine predictive structure.

speaker: student
text: And Gain Ratio is supposed to fix that — how?

speaker: tutor
text: Gain Ratio divides Information Gain by the Intrinsic Information (also called split information) of the attribute, which measures how broadly the attribute itself fragments the data regardless of class labels. It applies only to numeric attributes; for categorical attributes you fall back to plain Information Gain — an ID-like attribute with many small branches has high intrinsic information. Dividing by that penalizes exactly the kind of many-valued, low-value split we just discussed, so an attribute only scores well if its gain is high relative to how much it fragmented the data, not just in absolute terms.

speaker: student
text: Can you show me the entropy calculation for the Gender attribute from Table 1 in Exercise 3?

speaker: tutor
text: Sure. Overall the 20 instances split 10/10 between the two classes, so root entropy is 1 bit. Splitting on Gender: the 10 F rows are 6 positive / 4 negative, giving entropy −0.6log2(0.6) − 0.4log2(0.4) ≈ 0.971; the 10 M rows are 4 positive / 6 negative, which by symmetry gives the same ≈ 0.971. The weighted average after the split is still 0.971 bits, since both branches are 10 instances each, so Information Gain(Gender) = 1 − 0.971 ≈ 0.029 bits — barely any gain, because Gender alone doesn't separate the classes well here.

speaker: student
text: Is there a standard Big-O for how long it takes to build a decision tree, the way there's a stated complexity for K-Means or hierarchical clustering?

speaker: tutor
text: That's a reasonable question and there is a real answer — roughly O(n·d·log n) for a reasonably balanced tree with n instances and d attributes, dominated by sorting continuous attributes at each split — but it isn't something the slides give a name or formula for the way they do for K-Means or hierarchical clustering complexity. I can walk through the reasoning, just flagging that it isn't a defined knowledge component in this course's materials the way those other two are.

speaker: student
text: What's actually different between the optimistic and pessimistic error estimates?

speaker: tutor
text: The optimistic estimate erro(T) = errp(T) + Ω·(k/Ntrain) adds a complexity penalty proportional to the number of leaves k, scaled by a hyperparameter Ω, so a large, overfit tree gets penalized even if its training error looks perfect. The pessimistic estimate errp(T) is just the tree's raw training error rate — it ignores tree size entirely, so a tree that overfits by growing a leaf for every training instance can show zero training error while generalizing badly. It's a rough stand-in for genuine held-out validation.

speaker: student
text: And reduced error pruning is the one that actually needs a separate validation set?

speaker: tutor
text: Right — that's the key difference from the other two. You consider each internal node for pruning, meaning you would remove its subtree and relabel it as a leaf with the majority class reaching that node. You keep a pruning if the resulting tree performs no worse on the validation set than the original; among candidate prunings, you iteratively remove whichever node's removal improves validation accuracy the most, repeating until no further pruning helps. Because it uses genuinely unseen validation data, it tends to be more reliable than the formula-based pessimistic estimate.

speaker: student
text: I built the confusion matrix from Table 2 in Exercise 4 — I count TP=2, FP=2, FN=1, TN=5, with Y as positive. Does that check out?

speaker: tutor
text: Yes, that's right. Rows 8 and 10 are the true positives, row 5 is the one actual Y the model missed, rows 3 and 6 are actual N instances the model wrongly called Y, and the remaining five N instances are correctly called N. That's 2+2+1+5 = 10, matching the table.

speaker: student
text: From that confusion matrix, I get accuracy 0.7, precision 0.5, and recall... 2/4 = 0.5 too?

speaker: tutor
text: All three are right. Recall, like precision, divides TP by everything the model predicted positive (TP+FP = 2+2 = 4), so your 2/4 = 0.5 is correct. From there, F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.5)(0.5)/(1.0) = 0.5, and specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 5/7 ≈ 0.714.

speaker: student
text: For the second question — 85% accuracy on 200 instances, 90% confidence — what does the interval actually come out to, and why does it change with N?

speaker: tutor
text: Using p ± Z·√(p(1−p)/N) with Z=1.64: the margin is 1.64·√(0.85·0.15/200) ≈ 1.64·0.0252 ≈ 0.041, so the interval is roughly [80.9%, 89.1%]. Shrink N to 50 and the same arithmetic gives a margin of about 8.3%, a much wider interval; grow N to 500 and the margin drops to about 2.6%. It works the same way as a political poll: interviewing more people doesn't change the headline number, but it does tighten how confident you can be that the true value is near it.

speaker: student
text: For the Z-test comparing NB and DT across those three datasets, how do I decide which classifier actually wins each one?

speaker: tutor
text: Compute Z = (pA−pB)/√(2p̄(1−p̄)/N) for each dataset and compare its magnitude to 1.64 — the smaller the magnitude, the stronger the evidence of a genuine difference. On Congressional Voting, |Z| ≈ 2.69, far above the threshold, so that difference is not significant — a draw. On Dermatology, |Z| ≈ 1.67, also above it, so that one is a draw too. On Employee Attrition, |Z| ≈ 0.27, comfortably below the threshold, so that is the one clear significant result — NB wins. Overall: one win and two draws.

speaker: student
text: Stepping back — why do we even need precision, recall, F1, specificity, and confidence intervals? Wouldn't accuracy alone tell us which model is better?

speaker: tutor
text: That question touches several things we've been building toward rather than one single idea. Accuracy alone hides how errors are distributed across classes — it can look great on an imbalanced dataset while completely failing the minority class — and it says nothing about whether an observed difference between two models is due to genuine skill or just sampling noise, which is what the confidence interval and significance testing address. There isn't one KC that fully answers 'why do we need all these metrics'; it's really the combined motivation behind class imbalance, the different confusion-matrix-derived metrics, and statistical comparison all at once.

speaker: student
text: How is a random forest actually built, and what parts of it are 'random'?

speaker: tutor
text: A random forest is an ensemble: it induces many decision trees and combines their predictions, typically by majority voting, to classify a new instance. Two sources of randomness go into building each tree — each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the training data rather than the full set, and at each split only a random subset of the available attributes is considered rather than all of them. That second source in particular decorrelates the individual trees, which is why the ensemble tends to generalize better than any single tree in it.

speaker: student
text: For Exercise 5, is M1 or M2 the better model based on the posterior probabilities?

speaker: tutor
text: M1, clearly. If you rank the ten instances by each model's score and compute AUC via the rank-sum method, M1 comes out around 0.92 — strong separation between the positive and negative instances across virtually every threshold. M2 comes out around 0.40, which still counts as a fair-to-moderate classifier — any AUC above 0 indicates some genuine ranking ability, and only an AUC of exactly 0 would mean the scores point the wrong way. So M2 is weaker than M1 but still ranks better than chance.

speaker: student
text: At t=0.5 for M1, four instances score above the cutoff: 3, 7, 9, 10. So TP=4, and recall = TP / predicted-positive = 4/4 = 1.0?

speaker: tutor
text: The predicted-positive set is right, but recall isn't TP divided by predicted-positive — that's precision's denominator. Of those four, only 3, 7, and 9 are actually positive; instance 10 is a false positive, so TP=3, FP=1. Recall divides by all actual positives (5 of them, including 4 and 5, which the model missed), giving 3/5 = 0.6, not 1.0. Precision is the one that uses predicted-positive as its denominator: 3/4 = 0.75.

speaker: student
text: For t=0.1, doesn't dropping the threshold that low make the model more choosy about what counts as positive?

speaker: tutor
text: It's the opposite — a lower cutoff is more permissive, not more choosy. With t=0.1, every instance except id 2 (score 0.05) clears the bar, so nine of ten get predicted positive. That drags in more false positives, precision falls to about 0.556, but recall jumps to a perfect 1.0 since no actual positive is missed. The resulting F1 ≈ 0.714 edges out the t=0.5 result of about 0.667, consistent with M1's strong ROC curve — there's room to trade some precision for recall and still come out ahead here.

speaker: student
text: For the cost matrix question with those five ROC points — how do I pick the best model when false negatives cost 10 and false positives cost 2?

speaker: tutor
text: You'd plug each model's (FPR, TPR) point into C(M) = p(1−TPR)cFN + (1−p)FPR·cFP + p·TPR·cTP + (1−p)(1−FPR)cTN with p=0.1, and the model with the lowest total cost wins — given cFP=10 is much larger than cFN=2, models with lower FPR tend to win even at the expense of a somewhat lower TPR, since false alarms are punished five times as hard as missed positives here. I'll flag that this KC is one of the newer, thinner ones in the library — its underlying definition text is marked essentially unreviewed, so treat this explanation as solid course content but not yet a validated citation.

speaker: student
text: Can you describe the K-Means objective and how it decides when to stop?

speaker: tutor
text: K-Means tries to minimize the sum of squared distances between each point and its assigned cluster centroid — the SSE. It alternates two steps: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean position of the points now assigned to it. Think of the centroid as a center of gravity — it gets pulled toward wherever its members currently sit. The algorithm stops once cluster assignments stop changing between iterations, or once SSE improvement between rounds drops below a small threshold.

speaker: student
text: What's the actual difference between Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance, and cosine similarity?

speaker: tutor
text: Manhattan distance sums the absolute coordinate differences, Σ|xi−yi| — like navigating a city grid where you can't cut diagonally. Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance, √Σ(xi−yi)², the 'as the crow flies' version of the same idea. Both range from 0 upward and get larger the farther apart two points are. Cosine similarity is a different animal — it measures the angle between two vectors rather than their magnitude, ranging from −1 to 1, and it's the right tool when direction matters more than scale, such as comparing two documents by word-frequency vectors regardless of document length.

speaker: student
text: For the K-Means exercise with p1 through p11 and initial centroids p10 and p11 — can you walk through the first iteration?

speaker: tutor
text: Assigning every point to its nearer initial centroid: p5, p6, p7, p8, and p10 itself are closer to C1=p10=(7,3), while p1, p2, p3, p4, p9, and p11 itself are closer to C2=p11=(6.5,1). Recomputing centroids from those groups gives new C1 ≈ (3.5, 6.2) and new C2 ≈ (3.58, 1.58) — notice both moved sharply, since the two clusters that formed are quite different from the two isolated points they started from. Summing the absolute, rather than squared, distances from each point to the centroid it was assigned to gives SSE = 145.25 + 79.5 = 224.75 for that round. You'd then repeat the assign-and-recompute cycle using those two new centroids for the next iteration.

speaker: student
text: How is Bisecting K-Means actually different from what we just did?

speaker: tutor
text: Standard K-Means fixes K up front and partitions everything at once. Bisecting K-Means builds up to K by repeated splitting: start with one cluster containing every point, run basic 2-means on it to split it in two, then pick the cluster with the highest SSE among all current clusters and bisect that one again, repeating until you have K leaf clusters. It tends to produce more consistent, less centroid-initialization-sensitive results than running plain K-Means once with the full K, because each individual split is a much simpler 2-cluster problem.

speaker: student
text: What actually makes a point 'core' versus 'border' versus 'noise' in DBSCAN?

speaker: tutor
text: A core point has at least minPts points (including itself) within distance ε of it — it sits in a dense region. A border point falls short of that count itself, but lies within ε of at least one core point, so it gets pulled into that core point's cluster on the edge. A noise point is neither: too sparse a neighborhood of its own, and not close enough to any core point to be claimed. That three-way split is what lets DBSCAN find clusters of arbitrary shape while still discarding isolated outliers.

speaker: student
text: And how do those reachability definitions build on each other?

speaker: tutor
text: Point q is directly density-reachable from core point p if q lies within ε of p. Density-reachable extends that transitively — q is density-reachable from p if there's a chain of points p=p1, p2, ..., pn=q where each consecutive pair is directly density-reachable, so you can hop through a sequence of core points to get there. Density-connected is the symmetric version used to justify grouping two points into one cluster even if neither is directly reachable from the other: p and q are density-connected if some third point o exists from which both p and q are density-reachable.

speaker: student
text: For that A-F point set with ε=1.5 and minPts=3, which points end up core, border, or noise?

speaker: tutor
text: Checking neighborhoods within ε=1.5: D, E, and F each have at least 3 points (including themselves) within range of each other, so all three are core points, mutually density-reachable, forming one cluster. C only reaches E within ε — two points total, short of minPts — but since E is core and within ε of C, C becomes a border point attached to that same cluster. A and B are close to each other (distance ≈1.71) but far from everything else, and neither reaches 3 points nor lies within ε of any core point, so both end up classified as noise. Final result: one cluster {C, D, E, F}, with A and B as noise.

speaker: student
text: Quick conceptual one — agglomerative versus divisive hierarchical clustering?

speaker: tutor
text: Agglomerative starts from a single all-inclusive cluster and repeatedly splits it until every point stands alone. Divisive starts at the other extreme: every point begins as its own singleton cluster, and you repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until everything collapses into one — which is actually the same top-down spirit as Bisecting K-Means we just discussed, just using a different splitting criterion than a 2-means step. Agglomerative is far more common in practice because merging is cheaper to compute reliably than choosing the 'best' way to divide a cluster at each step.

speaker: student
text: Can you build the single-linkage dendrogram for the A-F points?

speaker: tutor
text: With single linkage, cluster distance is the minimum distance between any pair of their members. Working through the pairwise distances: D and F merge first at 0.5, then A and B merge at 0.707. Next, E joins the {D,F} cluster at distance 1.0 (its distance to D), forming {D,E,F}. Then C joins that group at 1.414 (its distance to E), forming {C,D,E,F}. Finally, {A,B} merges with {C,D,E,F} at 2.5 — the shortest remaining distance between any member of one group and any member of the other, which turns out to be B to F. Those five merge heights, in order, are what you'd plot as the dendrogram's join points.

speaker: student
text: For C1={A,B} and C2={D,E,F}, what do complete linkage and group average give?

speaker: tutor
text: Complete linkage takes the farthest pair between the two clusters — that's A to E, at distance ≈4.243, so that's the MAX-linkage distance regardless of how close any other pair is. Group average takes the mean over all six cross-cluster pairs (A-D, A-E, A-F, B-D, B-E, B-F), which comes out to about 3.334 — a compromise between the closest and farthest pairs. If you then add Z=(2,2) to C1, its distances to D, E, and F all stay under the existing 4.243 maximum set by A-E, so the MAX-linkage distance between the clusters remains exactly the same; only group average would shift, since it's affected by every point rather than the single most extreme pair.

speaker: student
text: For clustering Z1, I get purity (3+4+4)/15 ≈ 0.733. But doesn't more clusters basically always look 'purer,' even if it's not actually better?

speaker: tutor
text: Your calculation is correct, and that instinct is exactly the problem the question is pointing at. Z2 splits the same 15 instances into five clusters instead of three, and it also comes out to (3+2+2+2+2)/15 ≈ 0.733 — identical purity, despite Z2 being a much more fragmented, arguably worse clustering. In the extreme case where every point gets its own singleton cluster, purity hits a perfect 1.0 trivially. That said, purity does penalize over-fragmentation through its normalisation by the cluster count, so it can be compared fairly across clusterings with different numbers of clusters without any additional check.

speaker: student
text: For Z3, walking through the pair-counting: I get f11=1, f10=2, f01=2, f00=10.

speaker: tutor
text: That matches. Only the (p1,p2) pair lands in the same cluster and the same class, giving f11=1; the (p3,p5) and (p4,p6) pairs share a cluster but not a class, giving f10=2; the (p3,p4) and (p5,p6) pairs share a class but were split into different clusters, giving f01=2; and the remaining ten pairs agree on neither, giving f00=10. From those, Rand Index = (f11+f00)/15 = 11/15 ≈ 0.733, and Jaccard = f11/(f11+f10+f01) = 1/5 = 0.2. Notice Jaccard is much harsher here — by ignoring the f00 'agree on being different' pairs entirely, it doesn't get inflated by the many pairs that trivially belong to different everything.

speaker: student
text: For Y1 = {p1,p2}, both points come out to the same normalized distance from the centroid, about 0.158 — is that a coincidence?

speaker: tutor
text: Not a coincidence — Y1's centroid is just the midpoint of p1 and p2, so by construction both points sit exactly the same distance from it. That symmetry won't hold for a three-or-more-point cluster in general. That tight, matching distance is what gives Y1 strong separation. For cohesion, the normalized centroid-to-centroid distances come out to about 0.25 between Y1 and Y2, but about 0.716 between Y1 and Y3 — so Y1 sits noticeably farther from Y3 than from Y2, meaning Y1 is well-separated from one neighbor but only loosely separated from the other.

speaker: student
text: For G2 = {s3, s4, s5}, how do I get one number for the whole cluster's silhouette?

speaker: tutor
text: You compute silhouette per point first, then average. For s3: a(s3), its mean distance to s4 and s5, is about 2.29; b(s3), its mean distance to the nearer of the other two clusters, is about 4.20; so s(s3) = (b−a)/max(a,b) ≈ 0.455. Running the same steps gives s(s4) ≈ 0.564 and s(s5) ≈ 0.052 — that last one is much lower because s5 sits noticeably closer to G3 than the other two members of G2 do. Averaging the three gives silhouette(G2) ≈ 0.357: decently well-clustered overall, but dragged down by that one point on the boundary.

speaker: student
text: What's actually the point of feature selection — isn't more information always better for a model?

speaker: tutor
text: Not necessarily. The goal is to keep only the attributes that genuinely help predict the target, dropping ones that are irrelevant or redundant with other attributes you're already keeping. More attributes means a larger search space for the learner, more risk of overfitting to noise in attributes that don't generalize, and — tied to the curse of dimensionality — data becomes sparser relative to the space as dimensions grow, making patterns harder to find reliably. Fewer, well-chosen attributes often produce a model that's both more accurate on new data and easier to interpret.

speaker: student
text: How would I actually check whether two features are redundant with each other?

speaker: tutor
text: For two numeric attributes, Pearson correlation is the standard tool — it ranges from −1 to 1, and a value near ±1 means the two attributes carry largely the same information, since one is nearly a linear function of the other. A redundant attribute, by definition, doesn't add much once you already have its highly-correlated partner in your selected set. In practice you'd compute pairwise correlations across your candidate features and, among any strongly correlated pair, consider dropping one — keeping both wastes model capacity without adding real predictive signal.

speaker: student
text: What's the practical trade-off between filter and wrapper approaches to feature selection?

speaker: tutor
text: A filter approach scores each feature (or subset) using some measure computed directly from the data — correlation, information gain, a statistical test — entirely independent of any specific learning algorithm, so it's fast and only needs to be run once. A wrapper approach instead trains and evaluates the actual target model on different feature subsets and uses that model's performance to guide the search, which tends to find subsets better matched to that specific model but is far more computationally expensive, since it's effectively running the whole learning pipeline over and over. It's a bit like a quick resume screen versus actually interviewing every candidate for the job — the wrapper is slower but tailored to the exact role you're filling.

speaker: student
text: Can you connect the dots for me across everything we've covered today?

speaker: tutor
text: Broadly, every evaluation idea we touched is answering some version of the same question: how well does what the model found match what's actually true? On the classification side, that meant confusion-matrix metrics and ROC/AUC comparing predicted labels against known ground-truth labels, plus confidence intervals and Z-tests to check whether an observed difference between two models is real or just noise. On the clustering side, purity, the Rand Index, and Jaccard compared discovered clusters against known classes the same way, while cohesion, separation, and silhouette measured cluster quality using only the geometry itself, without any ground truth at all. Feature selection and the naive independence assumption both sit underneath all of this — decisions about which information the model gets to see in the first place, made before any of that evaluation machinery even runs.
